reviewType: Author's chemical and visual review; complements automated validation and any independent editorial review
originality: Questions, datasets, values and diagrams were authored for this bank. No third-party question-bank wording was copied.
scopeChecks: All 30 radical questions are SL because R3.3 has no additional HL material.
Ka, Kb, pOH, salt hydrolysis, buffers and weak-acid titration curves are HL.
Standard electrode potentials, aqueous electrolysis and electroplating are HL; molten electrolysis and organic redox are shared.
Detailed substitution, alkene addition and benzene electrophilic-substitution mechanisms are HL.
SL substitution questions use equations and electron-pair movement without requiring SN1/SN2 distinctions.
SN1/SN2 experimental rate-law questions use the explicit R2.2/R3.4 linking statements; they do not compare solvent or mechanism effects on relative rates.
The halonium intermediate is supplied for interpretation, not demanded as an extra memorized syllabus term.
No reagent-name recall, Faraday current-time calculations, quadratic acid equilibria, or electrophile-generation mechanism is required.
chemicalChecks: Acid/base and redox equations were checked for atom and charge conservation, including permanganate/iron and aluminium/silver balances.
Numerical acid/base, gas-volume, cell-energy and titration values were independently recalculated in check-r3.mjs.
Weak-acid/base and buffer approximations are explicit, and graph-reading pKa credit allows the plotted resolution.
Electrodes use oxidation/anode and reduction/cathode consistently across voltaic and electrolytic cases.
Organic products preserve valence, carbon skeleton and reaction conditions; further oxidation is distinguished using distillation and reflux.
Radical dots, one-electron arrows, initiation/propagation/termination identities, isotope labels and total atom counts were checked.
Curly-arrow tails start at the relevant electron pair or bond, and heads point towards the destination atom or forming bond.
SN2 inversion is distinguished from optical-rotation sign; equal SN1 enantiomer formation is conditioned on equal access to both faces.
Carbocation stability and hydration products agree; the benzene intermediate loses H+ and restores delocalization.
The bromonium ion has two lone pairs and two bonds at positively charged bromine; bromide has four lone pairs.

fixesDuringReview: Moved salt-bridge label to avoid the voltmeter and immersed the metal electrodes in their solutions.
Made the SN1 carbocation centre explicit so the nucleophile arrow cannot be mistaken for attack on an alkyl group.
Adjusted single-barbed arrowheads to follow the curve tangent.
Added correct lone-pair counts to the bromonium intermediate and bromide.
Added explicit wedge/dash SN2 inversion and benzene substitution worked figures.
